title: OK, maybe 2025 wasn't so great for ed reform
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: Petrilli reconsiders his optimism about 2025 as a year for education reform. Declining NAEP scores, persistent foundation neglect of urban schools, AI's likely exacerbation of inequality, and federal policy instability weigh heavily against scattered wins in state-level enrollment and refugee support policies. The fundamental question remains unresolved: whether real change will follow depends on whether policymakers prioritize education reform, whether candidates center it, and whether any efforts move student outcomes. Petrilli closes with a call to action, placing responsibility for 2026 squarely on the advocacy community's shoulders.
points: Student outcomes are the measure: Declining NAEP results make it difficult to declare any year successful for education reform.
Inequality is accelerating: Few major foundations invest in urban districts, and AI threatens to widen divides by income and race.
Scattered wins exist but lack systemic weight: State-level progress on enrollment and refugee support is real but insufficient without federal alignment.
Accountability shifts to advocates: Real change depends on whether individual leaders and advocates push for action in 2026.
quotes: The measure of any year is whether it was good or bad for kids. It's very difficult to call 2025 successful given the NAEP results released in late January.

There seems to be no effort or vision for how to better support most low-income kids in the biggest school districts. No major national foundations are seriously investing in improving schools in urban areas, and there are fewer now than the last two decades.
AI, while great for those with privilege and for some without privilege to accelerate their learning, seems to be a powerful accelerator for exacerbating the divides by income and race.

Federal actions have slashed data and research support and infrastructure. Making sure that all children have what they need to live up to their full potential remains one of the most important responsibilities we all have.

We probably won't be able to judge 2025 for a few years, once we know what follows. Do policymakers listen to the opinion leaders and start getting their acts together? Do candidates for president put ed reform front and center? And does any of this start to move the needle on student outcomes?” Archived from Schooled on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
